title: Esther: For Such a Time as This
lead: God can place a person where they are able to bring rescue to others.
questions: Who might be the reason you have ended up in the very place where you are right now?
Which “coincidences” of this past year look different once you assume that God works without a sound?
Whom with a life story like Esther’s, entangled and deeply at home in the world, have you crossed off God’s plans?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Esther is the only book of the Bible in which the name of God never appears. That is not a gap. It is a method: God’s hiddenness is the very foundation of its theology. This book tells of a time much like ours, with no prophets and no signs. And it shows that in such a time God does not work less. He works more quietly. Its heroine is an orphan of the diaspora who ended up in a harem, hid where she came from, and became the wife of a pagan king. The text passes no verdict on her: it does not praise, it does not condemn, it simply describes. Because this book is about God saving His people through imperfect people, placed where no pious committee would ever have put them.

When Haman obtained a decree to wipe out the Jews, Mordecai sent Esther a message that sets the whole story in motion: “If you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place… And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” He never spoke God’s name, but they both knew what he meant. Going in to the king unsummoned was punishable by death, and the king had not invited her in thirty days. Esther’s reply is one of the boldest statements in the Bible: “Fast for me… After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!” Her courage did not come from a sign, because there was none. It was the result of a decision made in the dark.

At the mathematical center of the book stands the smallest event imaginable: “That night sleep escaped the king.” The Hebrew says literally that sleep fled from the king. The form of the verb on its own, however, does not make clear who caused the sleeplessness. In the context of the book it can be read as the work of Providence. The turning point in a whole nation’s rescue is that someone could not sleep. Seen from the outside, Providence looks like chance. What happened next? Haman was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai, the people were given the right to defend themselves, and Purim was established in remembrance: a feast of rest, a memorial of the month in which “their sorrow turned to joy.” Most of our lives look like the book of Esther, not the book of Exodus. The absence of signs is not the absence of God.

Esther is the only book of the Bible in which the name of God never appears. There is no prayer in it, no temple, no sacrifice, no prophet; the only religious gesture left is fasting. Over the centuries some have seen this as a problem. Yet it is not a problem but a method: God’s hiddenness is the very foundation of this book’s theology. The rest of the Bible mostly tells of a God who speaks and acts in the open. This one book tells of a time much like ours: no prophets, no clear signs, and choices between bad and worse. And it shows that in such a time God does not work less, only more quietly.

sections.heading: An Orphan of the Diaspora
paragraphs: The heroine of today’s reading is named Hadassah; in Persian, Esther. An orphan with neither father nor mother, raised by her relative Mordecai in a family carried off from Jerusalem. She belongs to those who did not go home after Cyrus’s decree: she is part of the Jewish people scattered across the empire and settled comfortably in a foreign land. Her road to the throne has nothing in common with a prophet’s call. She is taken into the royal harem because of her beauty, hides her ancestry because her guardian told her to, and becomes the wife of a pagan ruler, though the Law forbade such marriages. A reader raised on the story of Daniel may wince: in Babylon he refused the food from the king’s table, and she keeps silent even about who she is. Here we need to stress something rare: the text passes no verdict on her at all. It does not praise, it does not condemn, it simply describes. Because this book is not about what heroes ought to be. It is about a God who is able to save His people through imperfect, entangled people, placed where no pious committee would ever have put them.

sections.heading: Where Homage Ends
paragraphs: The crisis begins with a bow that is refused. The king promotes Haman and orders everyone to kneel before him, but Mordecai “would not bow down or pay homage.” This was not plain stubbornness. The Hebrew verbs used here can describe both bowing before people and religious worship, so the language alone does not settle Mordecai’s motive. The Bible does, however, stress his steady refusal and his Jewish identity. So we can speak of a line he recognized: respect for authority is right, until authority demands what belongs to God alone. The offended official’s revenge at once takes in an entire people. Haman obtains from the king a decree to destroy every Jew in the empire, and he picks the date of the slaughter by casting pur, the lot. There is a bitter irony here: a man planning to exterminate God’s people casts lots because he believes someone is steering reality. He was right. He just didn’t know who. The chapter ends with one of the coldest sentences in the Bible: “Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.” A nation’s death warrant is signed, and the gentlemen sit down to drink.

sections.heading: Who Knows? For Such a Time
paragraphs: Chapter 4 is the heart of the book. Mordecai lies at the gate in sackcloth, and throughout the empire the Jews “fasted, wept, and lamented.” Notice how the author writes about prayer without mentioning it: elsewhere in the Bible these same words describe repentance before God; only the One addressed has been left out of the frame. Esther, living in the palace, is the last to find out. And Mordecai sends her a very direct message: “Do not imagine that because you are in the king’s palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews. For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” From another place. Mordecai does not say God’s name, but he and Esther both know what he means. And in the Bible, “who knows” is the phrase of people reaching for an uncertain hope: David said it over his sick child, and so did the king of Nineveh in the ashes. The trouble was that going in to the king unsummoned was punishable by death, and the king had not invited Esther in thirty days. Her answer is one of the boldest statements by a woman in Scripture: “Go and assemble all the Jews… and fast for me… After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!” The orphan from the harem, whom no one had ever asked about anything, takes command: now she is the one giving Mordecai orders, and he “went and did all that Esther had instructed him.” Her courage was not the result of a sign from heaven, because there was none. She made her decision in the dark, after three days of fasting, turned toward a God who was silent. The narrator adds a quiet reversal that frames the whole book: the story began with Queen Vashti, who would not come to the king when she was summoned. It is brought to its turning point by a queen who came without being summoned. That refusal cost a crown; this entrance saved a nation.

sections.heading: A Sleepless Night at the Center
paragraphs: The book of Esther is built symmetrically: the second half reverses the first, so that the exalted fall and the humbled rise. And at the mathematical center of this structure the author placed the smallest event imaginable: “That night sleep escaped the king.” The Hebrew says literally that sleep fled from the king. The verb itself, however, does not clearly point to a hidden agent behind this sleeplessness. In the context of the whole book it can be read as the work of Providence. From there the coincidences pile up far beyond anything chance could explain. The sleepless king has the chronicles read to him, and they happen to reach the record of the plot Mordecai had once exposed. It turns out he was never rewarded. And just then Haman happens to be standing in the court, having come to ask that Mordecai be hanged on the gallows he has already set up. So it is Haman who, the next day, must lead the horse carrying Esther’s guardian dressed in royal robes, proclaiming before him the very words he had composed for himself. The turning point in the rescue of an entire nation is that someone could not sleep. We have already seen this in the book of Ruth: God’s Providence, seen from the outside, cannot be told apart from coincidence. Esther supplies the other half of the lesson: Providence is at work even when no one sees it, names it, or feels it.

sections.heading: The Banquet and the Gallows
paragraphs: First, though, came the entrance itself. “On the third day, Esther put on her royal attire and stood in the inner court of the palace,” facing the throne, in the place where the unsummoned died. The king “extended the gold scepter in his hand toward Esther,” and she approached and touched its tip. Between those two sentences lies the whole terror of the moment: for an instant Esther’s life depended on the gesture of someone else’s hand. That is how it looked from the outside, because the reader of this book already knows whose hand was really directing the scene. At the second banquet Esther lays everything bare in a single breath: “Grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request. For my people and I have been sold out to destruction, death, and annihilation.” The queen who had hidden her ancestry for years binds her fate to the fate of the condemned: my people and I. From that moment events move like an avalanche. The terrified Haman begs for his life, falls onto the queen’s couch just as the king walks back in, and is then hanged on the gallows fifty cubits high built for Mordecai. The narrator plays here on a single Hebrew verb: Haman had boasted that the king had lifted him above everyone, and he did indeed end up hanging higher than anyone in Susa. Pride has a geometry in this book: the higher a man raises himself, the taller the gallows he builds for himself.

sections.heading: A Feast of Rest
paragraphs: One last obstacle remains: the king’s own law: a decree sealed with the royal signet ring could not be revoked even by the one who had issued it. The solution was a second edict: the right to self-defense. The text specifies that the aim was to repel attackers, not to take revenge, and it stresses that Mordecai’s people did not lay a hand on the plunder, even though the edict allowed it. Then “for the Jews it was a time of light and gladness, of joy and honor,” and, astonishingly, “many of the people of the land themselves became Jews.” The rescue turned out to be a missionary work. In remembrance, Purim was established, a feast named after the lots Haman cast: a memorial of the month “in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday,” kept with feasting, gifts to friends, and gifts to the poor. Notice what the Jews celebrate: not victory over an enemy, but rest from fear. The calendar of these events completes the picture. Haman’s lots were cast in the month of Nisan, the month of Passover, and it was around Passover that Esther fasted and went in to the king. So two books, Exodus and Esther, tell the same story in two modes: a people condemned to destruction, a mediator who intercedes at the risk of life, deliverance, and a new feast. Once God acts in a pillar of fire, once in someone else’s insomnia. Nothing limits Him in His choice of means. And one more thing deserves attention: Esther went in to the king “on the third day,” after three days of fasting for a people under sentence of death. Anyone who knows how the Bible goes on hears in that chord a foreshadowing: in Scripture, matters of life and death are settled on the third day.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: Most of a believer’s life looks like the book of Esther, not the book of Exodus. The sea does not part, fire does not fall, God does not speak in a voice you can hear. If you are in a chapter like that today, this book tells you: the absence of signs is not the absence of the Creator. He can be at work without a sound, in someone else’s sleepless night, in a coincidence, in the grammatical voice of a verb. Second, read Mordecai’s question again and address it to yourself. Your job, your home, your connections, even a position you reached by a crooked road, may be the place where God put you for the sake of someone’s rescue. “Who knows if perhaps” you are where you are “for such a time as this”? And third, for us as a community: God used a queen from a harem who hid her faith for years, and He did not wait until her life story measured up to Daniel’s. All around us are people with life stories like Esther’s: entangled, imperfect, deeply at home in the world. It is not for us to cross them off God’s plans. Sometimes they are the very ones standing closest to the place from which rescue comes.
